title: The Greywick Inheritance
subtitle: Greywick House above Haverkill, Dutchess County, New York, 15 to 22 October 1893

listing.title: The Greywick Inheritance 🕯️
listing.blurb: Hudson Valley, October 1893. Jasper Greywick, river freight and railroads, is three weeks in his grave, and his will is read by gaslight in the library of the house on the bluff: every person named in it must sleep seven nights under Greywick's roof before a penny is divided, and a sealed codicil waits for the eighth morning. The housekeeper takes every bedroom key. A lamp burns all night in the window of the closed wing. One heir never arrived, though his umbrella is in the hall stand. The house is keeping someone, and it has kept others before. Learn its rules before it learns your name. Levels 2–5.

synopsis: Greywick House stands on the bluff above the village of Haverkill on the east bank of the Hudson, eleven miles above Poughkeepsie: forty rooms of grey stone and Gothic gables built by Abram Greywick in the 1850s against an older house, a squat Dutch stone house of 1734 that the family calls the north wing and has kept shut for thirty-five years. The Greywick fortune began with towboats and barges at Haverkill Landing and grew into the Haverkill & Berkshire Railroad, which runs east from the Landing into Massachusetts. Abram's son Jasper Greywick died on 1 October 1893, aged fifty-nine, and was found at the foot of the north wing's stair. His will is read on Sunday 15 October, in the library, by gaslight, and it is strange: everyone it names, his widow Leonora, his sons Conrad and Linus, his daughter Honora, his nephew Ellis Callender, his doctor, a stage medium, his lawyer's clerk and a farm woman from Columbia County whom nobody has heard of, must sleep seven nights in a row beneath Greywick's roof, beginning that night, or forfeit what he left them. A sealed codicil is to be opened at nine on the morning of Sunday 22 October. The Panic of 1893 has gutted the railroad stocks, and the estate is worth a third of what the newspapers think. Everyone in the house needs the money. One of them has already killed for it. Linus Greywick, the younger son, never appeared for the reading; he came up from the station a night early, on Saturday 14 October, and the house has been keeping him ever since behind a door in the north wing that opens to one key only. In 1852 Abram Greywick locked his partner, Sabina Roelofs, the river captain who owned Haverkill Landing, in the upper room of her own stone house for seven nights while he recorded a forged deed to the Landing at Poughkeepsie, and on the seventh night she died there. She was never buried. Haverkill was told she was lost from the night boat. Now she keeps whoever is locked in behind a door at night in Greywick House, seven nights, as she was kept; she has kept the steward who killed her, Abram himself, and, three weeks ago, Jasper, whose own widow turned the key on him because he meant to confess and give the Landing back. Over seven nights and four scenarios, the reading and the first nights, the history in the town, the crypt and the county records, the night the house closes, and the seventh night, the party must learn the dead woman's rules and the living woman's lies, free Linus before his seventh dawn, keep the codicil out of the fire, and decide whether to lay Sabina Roelofs the only way her rules allow: by giving back what the Greywick fortune was built on.
hook: Haverkill station, Sunday 15 October 1893, twelve minutes past four in the afternoon. The up train from New York sighs to a stop on the river line beside the water, and you step down onto a plank platform with the Hudson a mile wide and pewter-grey at your back and the Catskills blue across it, the maples on the bluff gone red and yellow, and woodsmoke in the cold. A black-painted brougham with a crest on the door waits in the yard, its coachman in a mourning band. Up the hill, above the village roofs and the church spire, Greywick House shows its gables against the sky, every window dark but one: in a squat stone wing at the north end, low and old and out of keeping with the rest, a lamp is already burning in a window that faces the river, though it is broad daylight. You are named in a dead man's will. Some of you are family. Some of you have never met him. The letter that brought you, on the heavy cream paper of Strick & Garnet, Attorneys, Poughkeepsie, said only that your presence is required at the reading at eight o'clock this evening, that you should bring luggage for a week, and, in a postscript in a different hand, a shaky old man's hand: 'Do not lock your door.'

setting.name: Greywick House, the village of Haverkill and the river towns, Dutchess County, New York, 15 to 22 October 1893
setting.description: Haverkill, the Greywicks and everyone in this campaign are fictional; the Hudson Valley, Dutchess County, Poughkeepsie, the river line of the New York Central & Hudson River Railroad along the east bank, the Panic of 1893, the night boats, the ice harvest and the great river estates are real. Haverkill is a river village of nine hundred people, eleven miles north of Poughkeepsie: a railroad station and freight yards at the Landing on the flats, a main street climbing the hill with a general store, a hotel, the Haverkill Advertiser's office, an undertaker's, a livery and a telegraph office at the station; the Old Stone Church of 1717 with its churchyard; a district school; and above it all, on the bluff, Greywick House. The Landing is Haverkill's reason for being. It is the one deep-water landing on this stretch of the east bank, and since 1853 it has been the river terminus of the Haverkill & Berkshire Railroad, whose coal and freight yards fill the flats where the Roelofs family once beached sloops. Greywick House is two houses. The new one, built by Abram Greywick between 1855 and 1858, is a Gothic Revival pile of grey fieldstone with steep gables, carved bargeboards, a square tower, a conservatory and forty rooms lit by gas from the house's own gas machine in the cellar. Against its north end stands the old one, the Roelofs house of 1734: two storeys of rough stone with a steep roof, a great cellar kitchen with a hearth you could stand in, and one upper room, the river room, whose window looks straight down the bluff to the Landing. The family calls it the north wing. It has been shut since 1858. Its doors from the main house are kept locked by day, with nobody behind them, and every night since 1866 the housekeeper has carried a lit lamp up its stair and set it in the river window. The household in October 1893: Leonora Greywick, the widow; Conrad Greywick, the elder son, a vice-president of the Haverkill & Berkshire; the housekeeper Mrs. Judith Quell, whose father was steward here before her; the old groundskeeper Gerrit Brouwer; the parlourmaid Fanny Ruddock; a cook, a footman, a coachman and two maids; and, for the week, the executor Mr. Lemuel Strick of Poughkeepsie with his black dispatch box.
setting.atmosphere: Gothic, autumnal and close. Gaslight hissing in brass brackets and turning the faces in the library yellow; corridors that go dark beyond the last bracket; the smell of beeswax, coal smoke, wet wool and old stone; a long-case clock in the hall that everyone hears strike three. The river is always there, a mile wide below the bluff, grey by day, black at night with the lights of a night boat crawling down it and the whistle of the river line trains echoing off the Catskills across the water. October is clear frost at first, then fog in the valley, then a day of hard rain, then the storm. Leaves blow down the long drive and scratch on the terrace. The horror is slow and fair: a door that tries its own handle at three in the morning; frost on the inside of a keyhole; a woman's voice in Dutch behind a door nobody can open; scratches in old oak that were not there yesterday. Most of what frightens people in this house is other people: a widow who is kind to everyone, a son with a revolver and debts, a housekeeper who knows more than she says, a lawyer who will not open his box. Show less, later. Let the players imagine. The dead woman is not a monster; she is a person who was wronged and has rules, and the house is frightening because it remembers.

regions.name: Greywick House
regions.description: The main house of 1858: the great hall with its staircase and long-case clock; the library, two storeys of books with a gallery, gasoliers, and the strongroom behind a steel door where the family papers are kept; the drawing room, dining room, morning room and conservatory; Leonora's sitting room and bedroom on the first floor; the guest rooms along the south corridor (the Blue Room, the Rose Room, the Tower Room and others); the servants' wing, servants' stair and attics; the cellars with the wine vaults, the coal hole and the gas machine that makes the house's light. Every bedroom door has its key taken by Mrs. Quell on the first night, and an iron door wedge, 'for the draughts', lying on every threshold.

regions.name: The North Wing (the Roelofs house)
regions.description: The stone house of 1734, joined to the main house by a door on each floor. Downstairs: the cellar kitchen, low and vaulted, with the great hearth and its hearthstone; a pantry; the old front door to the bluff, nailed shut. Upstairs, up a steep enclosed stair of worn oak: a short landing and one door, the original 1734 oak door with a Dutch box lock as big as a Bible, into the river room. By day the river room is empty, dusty and very cold, with a sea chest under the window and a lamp on the sill. The doorframe, inside and out, is scored with tally marks. By night, when the house is keeping someone, the room on the other side of that door is the room as it was in October 1852.

regions.name: The Grounds and the Crypt
regions.description: Sixty acres on the bluff: a long carriage drive up from the village, crossing the ravine of the Greywick Kill on a timber bridge; lawns, an orchard, a walled kitchen garden, the coach house and stables, Gerrit Brouwer's cottage, the gas machine's air-pump house; and, at the end of the orchard where the bluff falls to the river, the Greywick crypt, a granite mausoleum with a bronze door. A steep footpath zigzags down the bluff to the Landing.

regions.name: Haverkill and Poughkeepsie
regions.description: Haverkill village: the station and the freight yards at the Landing, the old stone pier where Sabina Roelofs kept her sloop, Main Street climbing the hill, the Old Stone Church and its registers, the Haverkill Advertiser's bound files since 1838, Phineas Tuttle's undertaking parlour and his ledgers, the telegraph office, and Mrs. Annetje Vedder's cottage on Ferry Lane, where the oldest woman in Haverkill remembers 1852. Poughkeepsie is twenty-five minutes down the river line (eight trains a day, 35 cents): the Dutchess County Clerk's office in the courthouse, with its libers of recorded deeds, the steamboat company's office on the waterfront, and Strick & Garnet's chambers.

campaignRules.name: The Seven Nights
campaignRules.description: The campaign is a clock of seven nights, Sunday 15 to Saturday 21 October 1893, and the codicil is opened at nine on Sunday 22 October. Sunset is about 5:15 and sunrise about 7:10. The will's condition: every person named must be beneath Greywick's roof from sunset to sunrise each night, or forfeit; Mr. Strick and his clerk keep a register, signed at dusk and dawn. Days are free: the party can go down to Haverkill, out to the crypt, or to Poughkeepsie by train, and must be back by sunset. gw-scenario-001 is Sunday to Tuesday morning (nights 1 and 2); gw-scenario-002 is Tuesday to Thursday (nights 3 to 5: the town, the crypt in Wednesday's rain, the county records, the closed wing); gw-scenario-003 is Friday 20 October, the night the house closes (night 6); gw-scenario-004 is Saturday 21, the seventh night, and the reading of the codicil. A second clock runs inside the first: Linus Greywick was locked into the Blue Room on the night of Saturday 14 October and has been kept since; his seventh night is Friday 20, and at dawn on Saturday 21 he is found dead at the foot of the north stair unless his door has been opened. If the players do nothing, this happens. Sunday: the reading; Mrs. Quell takes the keys. Monday night: Conrad locks his door and is only just broken out at 3 a.m. by the footman. Tuesday: Leonora burns the last pages of Jasper's journal in her sitting-room grate. Wednesday: Conrad wires two hired guards up from Poughkeepsie; Leonora begins to carry the iron key on her chatelaine. Thursday night: Conrad tries to force Mr. Strick's dispatch box. Friday: a nor'easter takes out the carriage bridge over the Greywick Kill at four; Leonora has had the iron wedges gathered up and the lamp oil watered; at half past ten she doses Mr. Strick's toddy with chloral; at eleven she stops the gas machine; at midnight the river lamp gutters out and every door in the house begins to close; at one she takes the codicil from the sleeping lawyer's box, and his door, shut by the Juffrouw, holds him for three o'clock. Saturday dawn: Linus is found dead. Saturday night: at two Leonora fires the north wing with kerosene to burn Sabina's bones and the stone house; if it burns with Sabina unlaid, she is loosed into the whole house. Sunday: there is no codicil to read, and Leonora is the richest woman on the river.

campaignRules.name: The Juffrouw's Rules
campaignRules.description: GM only, until the players learn them; never change a rule once they know it. The household calls her the Juffrouw (Dutch: 'Miss'). She is Sabina Roelofs, river captain, owner of Haverkill Landing, kept seven nights in the river room and killed there on 10 October 1852; use the Bound Spirit entry for her, with these rules in place of its own. RULE 1, WHAT CALLS HER: after dark she comes to any door in Greywick House that is locked or bolted with a living person behind it, and at three in the morning she opens it from her side and takes them. Signs: the handle tries itself, frost on the keyhole, slow scratching at the bottom of the door, a voice in Dutch. Getting the door open before three cheats her. RULE 2, WHAT BARS HER: on any night the lamp burns in the river window, she does not walk beyond the north wing (except to a locked door); and she cannot close or hold a door that is held open with iron. When the lamp is out she walks the whole house, closes every door she passes and holds it shut (Athletics DC 18 to force), and anyone shut in a room at three is taken as if locked in. RULE 3, WHAT SHE DOES: whoever she takes she keeps seven nights in the river room as it was in 1852, alive, hungry and cold, heard behind the door at night; on the seventh dawn they are found dead at the foot of the north stair. Her door opens only to her own iron key, turned from outside between midnight and dawn by someone who is not afraid of her (WIS save DC 15, or the key will not turn this hour; an Occultist has advantage). The key is Jasper's; Leonora has it. RULE 4, WHAT LAYS HER: she rests when her door is opened with her own key, her true name is spoken in the river room by one of the blood that kept her (a Greywick: Honora, Linus, Conrad, or Ellis Callender through his mother; not Leonora), and what was taken from her is given back in her hearing, by the codicil read aloud and accepted, or by a Greywick's signed deed returning the Landing to her heirs. Vulnerable to her true name (spoken to her face, it drives her from that room until the next night) and to daylight (she does nothing between sunrise and sunset). Ordinary weapons pass through her. Salt, holy water, prayers, mirrors and séances do nothing to her; a wrong rite costs the one who tried a point of Dread, and she knows they tried. Fire does not lay her: if the stone house burns with her unlaid, she is loosed into all of Greywick House. Three clues to each rule are named in the control file and in each scenario.

campaignRules.name: Dread and Rites
campaignRules.description: Use dread.json. Tell each player their Dread whenever it changes. Fear checks (WIS saves) in this house: DC 10 for the signs (the handle trying itself, frost on a keyhole, the voice behind the north door, a new tally mark in the oak); DC 15 for seeing her (a woman in a grey wool dress and a captain's pea jacket, her hair wet with rain, standing very still at the end of a corridor, or at the foot of a bed, with her back to you); DC 20 for the truth of it (the river room as it was in 1852; her face; a kept person brought out; Jasper's hands in the coffin). Darkness adds 2; knowing one of her rules lowers the DC by 2; the same horror costs Dread once per scene. Recovery as dread.json: a lit, safe room with company, the drawing-room fire, Mrs. Jansen's coffee, the Reverend's company. Laying her drops everyone present to 0. The light goes out at the worst moment once per scenario, and in gw-scenario-003 that moment is the river lamp. Rites are not magic: the lamp, the iron wedge, her name and her key work only because her rules say so. Before play, ask what the players do not want in the game; honour any 'skip that' at once by cutting away. The kept are adults; there are no children in Greywick House.

campaignRules.name: The Household
campaignRules.description: The living are as dangerous as the dead, and each has a reason. Leonora Greywick, the widow, killed her husband by locking his door on 24 September and has kept Linus since the 14th; she wants the codicil burned before Sunday. Conrad Greywick has embezzled $86,000 from the railroad's sinking fund, needs his fifth at once, carries a pocket revolver and believes someone is trying to cheat him, which is true. Mrs. Quell keeps her dead father's secret and the house's rules, and will lie to protect both. Mr. Strick will not open his box before the hour and is afraid of everyone. Run the murder on the three-clue rule: core clues are found by anyone who looks in the right place with the right skill, no roll; rolls add detail, speed or safety; a failed roll costs time before sunset, a point of Dread, or someone's trust, never the truth. Under the forfeiture clause, any heir who leaves or dies enlarges the others' shares; say so at the reading, and let the players watch everyone do the sum. If the table is stuck, have a companion lay it out by the drawing-room fire: who had the key, who turned the doctor away, who was in New York, whose door was locked, and who gains if the codicil burns.

explorationRules: This is a haunted-house sandbox with a town beside it, and the map is a schematic of the bluff, the village and the river line. The unit of time is the half-day by day and the hour by night. By day the party may go anywhere: the house and the closed wing (the north wing doors are locked, but Mrs. Quell, Gerrit and the strongroom key board have keys, and nothing in the stone house can hurt anyone in daylight), the grounds and the crypt, Haverkill village (twenty minutes' walk down the drive, ten by carriage, or the steep bluff path to the Landing), and Poughkeepsie (twenty-five minutes by train; trains at 7:40, 9:15, 11:30, 1:05, 3:20 and 4:12 up, roughly the same down). Everyone named in the will must be under Greywick's roof by sunset, about 5:15; the register is signed in the hall. The Seven Nights (campaignRules) are the engine: the household acts on its schedule, and every night has something in it. Nights are played hour by hour from dinner at seven: who sleeps where, who keeps watch, who walks the corridors, what is heard at three. The Juffrouw follows her rules exactly; the GM should play them as fixed facts the players can test and trust. The living do not: Leonora is warm, devout-seeming and helpful, Conrad is loud and frightened, Mrs. Quell is courteous and closed, Strick is stiff and honest. Run interviews across a dinner table, a kitchen table or a sickbed. Money is 1893 dollars: a housemaid earns $14 a month, a train ticket to Poughkeepsie is 35 cents, a room at the Haverkill Hotel $1.50, a telegram 25 cents for ten words, and the Greywick estate, after the Panic, is worth about $1,100,000, of which the Landing yards and their railroad lease are $420,000. Let the house breathe between frights: the clock in the hall, rain on the conservatory glass, a night boat's searchlight sweeping the bluff, Mrs. Jansen's bread, the Reverend's whist, the river under the moon. The players should come away knowing who Sabina Roelofs was, and having chosen what the Greywicks owe her.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. It does not change because a player has a better theory, and the Juffrouw's rules do not change once the players learn them. Greywick House, Haverkill, the Haverkill & Berkshire Railroad, Strick & Garnet and every person in this campaign are fictional. The Hudson Valley, Dutchess County, Poughkeepsie and its county clerk's office, the Hudson River Railroad (opened along the east bank in 1851) and the New York Central & Hudson River line it became, the river night boats, the New York Married Women's Property Act of 1848, the Panic of 1893 and the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago are real; no real person appears.
controlFile.theTruth: Hendrick Roelofs owned Haverkill Landing, the stone house above it (built by his grandfather in 1734), four hundred acres of the bluff, the sloop Zwaluw and half the Roelofs & Greywick Towing Line. When he died in 1847 it all passed to his elder daughter, Sabina, born 1821, who had sailed with him since she was twelve, held a master's ticket, and signed every paper she ever signed with her name and a small drawn anchor. Her partner, Abram Greywick, born 1806, a widower with a son, Jasper, ran the towboats. In 1851 the Hudson River Railroad opened along the east bank, and Abram saw the fortune: a railroad east from Haverkill Landing into the Berkshires, with the Landing as its river terminus. Sabina would not sell; she meant to keep the Landing open to the sloopmen and the farmers as her father had. Abram began forging her name, first on notes to buy railroad stock, then on a deed. On Saturday 2 October 1852 Sabina wrote to her sister Marritje Oudekerk in Columbia County: 'A. has been signing my name. I go down to Poughkeepsie to the courts on Monday.' On the night of Monday 4 October, Abram and his steward Jotham Quell locked her in the upper room of her own house, the river room, and turned away her housemaid, Annetje, with a month's wages. Abram meant to hold her only until the forged deed, dated 4 October, was recorded and the railroad's commissioners had met, and then to offer her money and a fait accompli. He recorded the deed at the Dutchess County Clerk's office in Poughkeepsie on Friday 8 October. For seven nights the eighteen-year-old Jasper carried her meals up the stair and set them by the door and did not open it, and she scratched one mark a night into the oak frame with a hairpin. On the seventh night, Sunday 10 October, in a storm, she got the window open and was half out of it, fifty feet above the river, when Jotham Quell came in to stop her; in the struggle she fell back and struck her head on the hearth, and died. Abram and Quell buried her under the hearthstone of the cellar kitchen. Haverkill was told she had taken the night boat to New York on Tuesday 5 October and must have been lost overboard; the Haverkill Advertiser printed it on 16 October, and printed on 23 October, unnoticed, the steamboat company's statement that no such passenger had been booked. Her estate was never probated; her sister was told she had drowned. The Haverkill & Berkshire was chartered in 1853 with the Landing as its terminus, and the Greywick fortune was made. Sabina Roelofs did not rest. She keeps, as she was kept: whoever is locked behind a door at night in her house, or the house built against it, she takes into the river room as it was in 1852 and keeps seven nights, and on the seventh dawn they are found at the foot of the north stair. In October 1853 Jotham Quell, who had taken to bolting his door, was the first. In October 1871 the under-gardener Gerrit Brouwer slept off a drink in the stone house's pantry with the bolt shot; Jasper, who had found the river room's iron key in his father's desk and worked out half the rules, opened her door on the second night and Gerrit walked out. In October 1873 Abram Greywick, sixty-seven, bolted himself in his study during a storm; he had taken the key back from Jasper that summer and locked it in his own strongbox, Jasper was in Europe, and nobody else knew what it was for; Abram was found on the seventh morning; the Advertiser called it apoplexy. Jasper lived forty years with it: he forbade locked doors, had Mrs. Quell (Jotham's daughter) light a lamp in the river window every night because he had noticed the Juffrouw kept to the stone house when the window was lit, put iron wedges on every threshold, carried the key on his watch chain, put up a tablet to Sabina in the crypt, and never said her name aloud. In 1893, ill, the railroad stocks collapsing in the Panic, and after a summer of sittings with a Brooklyn stage medium who told him 'she wants her name', he decided to confess. He traced Marritje's descendants through Strick and found her granddaughter, Dorothea Oudekerk, a farm woman at Claverack. On 9 September he signed a new will with the seven-nights condition ('I ask it as she was asked it'), meaning his children to learn her rules and lay her, and a sealed codicil confessing everything, returning the Landing yards and the railroad lease to Sabina's heirs, ordering an audit of the railroad's sinking fund (he had found Conrad's theft), and asking his children to open her door with her key and say her name. On 23 September he told his wife. On the night of Sunday 24 September, Leonora Greywick gave him his chloral drops, took the iron key off his watch chain, and locked his bedroom door from outside. He was kept seven nights. She told the household he was ill and would see no one, nursed him herself behind a door that had nobody behind it, turned Dr. Wyle away on 26 September, and told Mrs. Quell, who heard his voice behind the north door on the 27th and was too frightened to say so, that it was nonsense. At dawn on Sunday 1 October Jasper was found at the foot of the north stair; Dr. Wyle wrote apoplexy. Leonora put the key back on the chain for the body, then asked the undertaker for it on 3 October 'as a keepsake'. Jasper was buried on 4 October. Leonora then read the journal Jasper kept, learned three of the four rules, and burned what she did not like. Linus Greywick, Jasper's younger son, a bridge engineer, had a letter from his father written on 20 September; he came up from Chicago a night early, on the last train of Saturday 14 October, and walked up the hill in the rain. Leonora met him in the hall, put him in the Blue Room, waited until he slept and locked his door. At the reading she says he telegraphed that he was delayed. Her plan: let the house keep Linus and anyone else who learns too much, take and burn the codicil before Sunday, burn the stone house and Sabina's bones, and inherit.
suspects: Leonora Greywick, 52, the widow, Jasper's second wife since 1873: the murderer. Gracious, devout-seeming, tireless in her care of everyone. Motive: the codicil gives the Landing, the estate's one sound asset after the Panic, to a farm woman, and Jasper meant to publish his confession; she would be left with a fifth of very little and a name everyone on the river would whisper. She knows Rules 1 to 3 from Jasper's journal; she burned the pages about Rule 4 without understanding them. She cannot lay Sabina: she is not Greywick blood. THIS IS WHAT SUCCEEDS IF NOBODY INTERFERES.

Conrad Greywick, 38, the elder son, vice-president and treasurer of the Haverkill & Berkshire: an embezzler, not a murderer. Took $86,000 from the sinking fund to cover margin calls in the spring of the Panic; the examiners are due in November. He fears the codicil exposes him, which it does. Armed with a pocket revolver from Tuesday, drinking, sure the house and the family are against him. He was in New York from 22 September to 2 October, and can prove it.

Mrs. Judith Quell, 61, housekeeper since 1866: keeps the house's rules and her father's secret. Jotham Quell told her on his last night of freedom in 1853, when she was a girl of twenty-one, that he had 'helped Mr. Abram with the Juffrouw' and that she lay under the cellar hearth. She heard Jasper behind the north door in September and did nothing, and cannot forgive herself. She will lie to stop anyone digging under the hearth or telling the town, until she learns what Leonora did.

Lemuel Strick, 64, executor, of Strick & Garnet: honest, timid, gouty, and the only living person who knows what the codicil says. He advised Jasper not to make it public. He will not open the box before nine on Sunday 22 October for any reason, and he will not say what is in it, but he keeps the box's key on his watch chain and sleeps with the box under his bed.

Linus Greywick, 31, the younger son, bridge engineer, lately at the World's Columbian Exposition: not a suspect but the kept one. Kept since 14 October in the river room. If freed, he is the witness who names Leonora: he heard the key turn and her voice through the door: 'Goodnight, Linus.'
redHerrings: Conrad. He had the strongest motive anyone can see: his father discovered the theft and wrote it into the codicil, and he has a revolver and a temper. He was in New York when his father was locked in: the Fifth Avenue Hotel's register, his broker, two telegrams sent from the city on 27 and 29 September and a dinner at Delmonico's on the 30th. He is guilty of something else.
Mrs. Quell. She has every key in the house, she lights the lamp, she lies about the north wing, and she knew Jasper was missing. She is guilty of silence and of her father's crime, not of this one.

Aurelia Tierney, the medium (a pregen; if not played, she is an NPC guest). A stranger with an odd bequest who knew too much about Jasper at her sittings because she bribed his coachman in July. A fraud with one true gift, not a killer.
The forfeiture clause makes every named person a suspect, the players included. Let the household say so.
clues: A. A LOCKED DOOR CALLS HER (Rule 1). A1: Mrs. Quell takes every bedroom key on the first night and will say only that Mr. Jasper never allowed a locked door after dark (gw-scenario-001). A2: the postscript on every invitation, in Jasper's shaking hand: 'Do not lock your door' (gw-scenario-001). A3: Conrad's locked door on Monday night: the handle trying itself, the frost, the scratching, and Conrad grey and silent when broken out at three (gw-scenario-001). A4: Linus's letter from his father, in his valise: 'Never lock a door in this house at night' (gw-scenario-001). A5: Gerrit Brouwer's story of 1871 (gw-scenario-002). A6: the Advertiser's files: Jotham Quell 1853 and Abram Greywick 1873, each found dead after seven days shut in (gw-scenario-002).

B. THE LAMP AND IRON BAR HER (Rule 2). B1: Mrs. Quell carries the lit lamp to the river window every dusk; it burns all night (gw-scenario-001). B2: an iron wedge on every threshold, 'for the draughts' (gw-scenario-001). B3: Gerrit: 'Mr. Jasper drove the poker in the jamb so she couldn't shut it on him' (gw-scenario-002). B4: Annetje Vedder: 'When the Juffrouw was home the lamp was in the river window, for the boatmen. A lit window meant the captain was home and resting' (gw-scenario-002). B5: Jasper's journal fragment: 'lamp lit, she keeps to her own house' (gw-scenario-002). B6: demonstration when the lamp goes out (gw-scenario-003).

C. LINUS IS IN THE HOUSE, KEPT. C1: his wet umbrella and his initials on a valise in the hall closet, found by Fanny on Sunday morning (gw-scenario-001). C2: the Haverkill station agent sold no ticket but took Linus's ticket stub off the last train on Saturday night and gave him directions up the hill (gw-scenario-001 or 002). C3: there was no telegram; the telegraph office has none (gw-scenario-001 or 002). C4: a man's voice behind the river room door at night, calling for Honora, or for his father (gw-scenario-001 to 003). C5: the tally marks in the river room doorframe: a new mark appears each night in fresh wood (gw-scenario-002). C6: the Blue Room's bed slept in and its key missing from Mrs. Quell's board (gw-scenario-001 or 002).

D. SHE IS SABINA ROELOFS (her true name). D1: the tablet in the crypt: 'Sabina Roelofs, partner in the Line, lost from the night boat October 1852', put up by Jasper in 1874 (gw-scenario-002). D2: the Old Stone Church register: baptism 1821, membership, and the consistory minute of 10 October 1852, 'Miss Roelofs absent; Mr. Greywick reports she has gone to New York' (gw-scenario-002). D3: the county clerk's deed: 'Sabina Roelofs, spinster, to Abram Greywick' (gw-scenario-002). D4: Annetje Vedder (gw-scenario-002). D5: Dory Oudekerk's family Bible: 'Sabina, my sister, went to the stone house October 4 1852 and never came home. She did not drown. M.' (gw-scenario-001, if Dory is played or arrives). D6: S.R. and an anchor cut into the river room's window sill, and her logbook of the Zwaluw in the sea chest (gw-scenario-002).

E. HER KEY OPENS HER DOOR (Rule 3). E1: Gerrit: Mr. Jasper let him out in 1871 'with an old iron key, a Dutch one, big as your hand' (gw-scenario-002). E2: the river room's 1734 box lock: no other key in the house fits, picks do nothing, and the door will not break at night (gw-scenario-002). E3: Tuttle's ledger: 'watch, chain and one small old iron key; key returned to Mrs. G. at her request, 3 Oct.' (gw-scenario-002). E4: Jasper's journal fragment: 'only her own key, from outside, and a steady hand' (gw-scenario-002). E5: Linus's letter: 'the key is on my chain' (gw-scenario-001).

F. ABRAM STOLE THE LANDING AND SHE DIED IN THE HOUSE. F1: the deed, dated 4 October 1852, recorded 8 October, signed without her anchor (gw-scenario-002). F2: her letter of 2 October to her sister: 'A. has been signing my name' (gw-scenario-001 or 002, Dory's Bible). F3: the Advertiser, 16 and 23 October 1852: lost from the night boat, and the steamboat company's statement that no Miss Roelofs was booked (gw-scenario-002). F4: Annetje: her trunk was still in the house and she was sent home with a month's wages on the Monday (gw-scenario-002). F5: the bones under the cellar hearthstone: a woman of about thirty, the skull broken at the back, a hairpin in the right hand (gw-scenario-002 or 004). F6: Mrs. Quell, once she turns: her father's words (gw-scenario-003 or 004). F7: the codicil (gw-scenario-004).

G. JASPER WAS KEPT, AND LEONORA LOCKED HIM IN. G1: Dr. Wyle's own memory: turned away by Leonora on 26 September; the body cold and stiff for hours when found; fingernails torn (gw-scenario-001, Wyle's sheet). G2: Tuttle's ledger: the key returned to Mrs. G. (gw-scenario-002). G3: Jasper's body in the crypt: oak splinters under the nails, the same oak as the river room door (gw-scenario-002). G4: Fanny Ruddock saw Mrs. Greywick turn the key in Mr. Jasper's door on the night of 24 September, 'because he walks in his sleep' (gw-scenario-002, once Fanny trusts the party). G5: the Blue Room key in Leonora's workbasket (gw-scenario-002 or 003). G6: the scorched journal pages in her sitting-room grate (gw-scenario-002). G7: Linus's word, if freed (gw-scenario-003). G8: Conrad's alibi removes the other obvious suspect (gw-scenario-002).

H. HOW TO LAY HER (Rule 4). H1: Jasper's journal fragment: 'her name in her room, by our blood, and what we took given back in her hearing' (gw-scenario-002). H2: Annetje: 'She never wanted a penny that was not hers. She wanted what was hers' (gw-scenario-002). H3: The Thin Place, or anyone in the river room at night: frost writing on the window, MIJN NAAM, GEEF TERUG ('my name; give back'), which Dory, Gerrit or the Reverend can read (gw-scenario-002 or 003). H4: Linus, freed: 'She said one word over and over. Terug. Back.' (gw-scenario-003). H5: the codicil (gw-scenario-004).
controlFile.theKeyClue: The players solve the haunting when they stop asking how to drive the Juffrouw out and start asking what was done to her; and they solve the murder when they ask who could have turned the key on Jasper and why the key went missing. Everything turns on the key. Mention the iron key on Jasper's watch chain at the reading (Strick lists the watch among the effects), let Tuttle's ledger say where it went, and let the players see it, once, on Leonora's chatelaine among her scissors and her vinaigrette. If the party reaches Friday without knowing the key exists, have Gerrit Brouwer come to them at dusk with his cap in his hands and tell them how he was let out in 1871.
controlFile.outcomes: There is no single right ending, only consequences. LINUS: freed before dawn on Saturday 21 October, he lives and names Leonora; if not, he is found at the foot of the north stair, and the party has lost the witness and the heir who loved his father. THE CODICIL: if it survives, Strick reads it at nine on Sunday: the Landing yards and their lease to the heirs of Sabina Roelofs (Dorothea Oudekerk and her two brothers), the sinking-fund audit, the confession, and the request to open her door. If Leonora burns it, Strick can swear to its contents as a lost codicil before the Surrogate in Poughkeepsie, and the heirs can still choose restitution of their own will. THE JUFFROUW: laid, if Rule 4 is met in the river room on the seventh night; the house is only a house afterwards, the cold goes out of the north wing, and everyone present drops to 0 Dread. Driven off with her name, she returns the next night. If the stone house burns with her unlaid, she is loosed into the whole of Greywick House and it keeps one person every October from then on; the family sells it within the year. LEONORA: on the evidence (Fanny's word, Tuttle's ledger, the key on her chatelaine, the Blue Room key, Linus's testimony, Wyle's findings), Constable Mabie can hold her for the Dutchess County grand jury; or the household can hush it, which is the Greywick way. CONRAD: the audit exposes him whether or not the codicil survives, unless the heirs choose to cover it; he can be brought to confess and make what restitution he can. THE FORTUNE: if the Landing is given back, the Greywicks are left comfortable rather than rich and Dory Oudekerk owns the railroad's river terminus; if it is not, they are rich, and they live in a house where the doors do not lock. EPILOGUE: whatever happens, the GM should end on the following spring, with the ice going out of the river, a lamp no longer burning in the north window, and a new stone in the Old Stone Church's yard with a name and a small carved anchor on it, or not.
